metric_rationale: The design contains three families of trials on which a lexicographic one-reason rule and a unit-weight counting rule make opposite (or differently determinate) commitments: (i) pairs 1-4, where the single top cue is pitted against a coalition of 1-4 lower cues; (ii) pairs 9-12, where the first discriminating cue sits lower in the cascade and all remaining cues favour the other option; and (iii) pairs 5-6, where the tally is exactly even so a counting rule must guess at 50/50 whatever its parameters, while the cue cascade is fully decisive. The metric pools exactly these trials (agreement controls 7-8 are excluded, since both rules pick the same option there and they only dilute the contrast) and reports the proportion of choices going to the option favoured by the first discriminating cue. Under Take The Best this is (1-eps)*sigmoid(beta)+eps/2 on every included trial, i.e. high (~0.85 averaged over the parameter ranges) and tight, because each subject contributes 80 trials. Under Tallying it is the complement of the tally-consistent probability on the directional-conflict trials (~0.09) and exactly 0.5 on the two tie pairs, giving ~0.17 overall. Both theories' per-subject spread is driven mainly by the lapse rate, which shifts the two values toward 0.5 by comparable, modest amounts, so the ~0.68 mean gap dwarfs the between-subject variance. Mirror-image pairs are included in equal numbers, so any A/B key bias cancels and cannot inflate or deflate the score for either theory.

Two diagnostic trial families are contrasted within subject, which cancels overall lapse/noise level and sharpens the model split.

(1) Tally-tie trials (pairs 7/8 and 9/10): each option wins exactly the same number of cues, so Tallying is forced to exactly 50/50 for ANY beta and epsilon, while TTB is decisive (cue .93 beats cue .60; cue .87 beats cues .78/.70). I score the proportion of choices for the TTB-designated winner here: 0.5 under Tallying (only binomial jitter over 24 trials), ~0.85 under TTB.

(2) Large-margin disagreement trials (pairs 3/4, 5/6, 11/12): the tally favours the coalition option by 2-4 cues while TTB's top discriminating cue favours the other option. I score the proportion of choices for the tally winner: high (~0.85-0.95) under Tallying because the softmax is driven by beta*margin, near 0.15 under TTB.

The metric is the difference (2) - (1). Tallying predicts a clearly positive value (~+0.35); TTB predicts a strongly negative value (~-0.70), and because under TTB both terms are driven by the same beta and epsilon they move in opposite directions, amplifying rather than blurring the gap. The tie term is parameter-free for Tallying, so my side's variance is dominated by binomial noise alone, keeping the per-subject estimate tight at N=25.

The metric is a parameter-free behavioural index restricted to trials where the two options win on EXACTLY the same number of cues (unit-tally ties) but where the validity-weighted margin is clearly non-zero (|d| >= 0.15 with squared validities; this selects the base pairs {H1,H2} vs {L2,L3}, {H1,L1} vs {M,L3}, {H2,L1} vs {M,L2} and their A/B mirrors, and discards the near-zero-margin pair {H1,L3} vs {H2,L1}). On these trials I score the proportion of choices for the option holding the higher-validity cue set.

Tallying's softmax over equal tallies is EXACTLY uniform for every value of beta and epsilon, so it predicts 0.50 with no parameter-driven between-subject spread at all (only binomial noise over ~36 such trials, var ~0.007). AVAI, in contrast, integrates the continuous weighted difference, so it should land at ~0.89-0.98 across the plausible gamma/beta ranges, again with small between-subject spread. The mean gap is ~0.43 with per-subject SDs under 0.09, giving a decisive Welch test at N=25. It is not trivially true of AVAI: any model that binarises cue-wise winners (Tallying, Equal-Weight on signs, coin-flip-on-ties) must yield 0.5, whereas any validity-weighted or lexicographic integrator yields values well above 0.5; the metric measures a real behavioural phenomenon (magnitude sensitivity on count-tied trials) rather than model fit.

The design contains tally-TIE trials (each option wins exactly the same number of expert comparisons) that nevertheless carry a LARGE validity-weighted margin: base 7 / its mirror, where one option wins only on the .97 expert and the other only on the .53 expert. Tallying's softmax is exactly uniform whenever the two counts are equal, for ANY beta and epsilon, so the predicted proportion of choices for the option holding the high-validity cue is exactly 0.50 \u2014 a parameter-free prediction. AVAI acts on the continuous weighted difference (d \u2248 +0.66 with gamma=2), giving p \u2248 0.95\u20130.99 for that same option across its whole parameter range. I deliberately exclude the other tie structure (H1+L3 vs H2+L1, |d| \u2248 0.02) via the 0.30 threshold, because both theories predict chance there and it would only dilute the contrast. Each subject contributes 12 such trials, so per-subject binomial noise is small (var of the proportion \u2264 0.021 for Tallying, ~0.003 for AVAI), while the mean gap is ~0.47 \u2014 large mean separation with tight per-subject spread. The metric is well defined on a single subject's slice and on the pooled frame.

This is the dominance-accuracy metric: the proportion of trials on which the subject picks the option favoured by EVERY discriminating expert row (trials 13-18 here: |D| = 2, 4, and 6, all cues agreeing). Under AVAI the weighted evidence difference on such trials is large and grows with the number of agreeing cues, so choice is at ceiling (p ~ 0.98-1.00 for any admissible gamma/beta, limited only by the small epsilon lapse). Under RDS the choice on a dominance trial is correct only when the subject does not lose the thread: the conflict-interference term forces guessing at rate 1-(1-eps0)*rho^(m-2), giving ~0.86 at |D|=2, ~0.72 at |D|=4 and ~0.63 at |D|=6, i.e. a pooled value near 0.74. The metric therefore has a ~0.25 mean gap. It is also tight per subject: 30 trials contribute per subject, and both theories' parameter ranges move the expected value by only a few points, so per-subject variance is essentially binomial (~0.007 for RDS, ~0.0003 for AVAI), which comfortably clears Welch's test at N=25. It is not trivially true for AVAI because unanimous-cue accuracy is a plain behavioural quantity that any one-reason or non-interfering model could equally produce at ceiling; only RDS's specific claim that difficulty grows with the COUNT of differing rows (rather than their diagnosticity) predicts a substantial sub-ceiling value here.

Isolates the 'crown jewel' trial family (design bases 3 and 4 and their mirrors: trials 5-8) via a purely structural filter: exactly two discriminating columns, pointing to opposite options, with the LATER column carrying the LOWER validity (0.95 early vs 0.55 late). On these displays the two theories make opposite, near-deterministic predictions.

AVAI integrates weighted validity, so it must pick the option holding the 0.95 cue regardless of column position: weighted difference |d| = 0.95^gamma - 0.55^gamma ~ 0.60, beta*|d| ~ 3-5, so p(later-cue option) ~ 0.02-0.05, essentially independent of where the rows sit. RDS instead lets recency x distinctiveness decide: the later, lower-validity row has salience ratio exp(lambda*5)*(0.45)^delta vs exp(0)*(0.05)^delta, i.e. thousands to one, so the later-cue option is picked with probability ~ (1-eps0) + eps0/2 ~ 0.85 (m=2 means minimal conflict interference).

Predicted values: ~0.85 under RDS vs ~0.03 under AVAI, a gap of ~0.8. Because 24 trials per subject enter the average and both theories are near-deterministic on them, per-subject variance is tiny (binomial ~0.005 for RDS, ~0.001 for AVAI, plus negligible parameter spread), so the contrast is both large in mean and tight across subjects. Crucially it is not trivially true for RDS: any position-blind integrator (including tallying, Bayesian weighting, or plain TTB) would land far below 0.5 here, so a value near 0.85 in humans is diagnostic of position-driven, redundancy-discounted one-reason choice.

The design duplicates every stated validity, so OCO-LI's individuation gate is exactly phi=0: the odd-cue-out/recency anchoring competition cannot run and choices collapse to a probability-matched tally over the discriminating rows. RDS has no such gate, so its salience weights exp(lam*j)*(1-v)^delta (spanning ~5 orders of magnitude here) make the LAST-READ discriminating row essentially decide the trial.

The metric is the rate of choosing the option favoured by the highest-index (last-read) discriminating row, computed only on conflict displays (at least one row favouring each option) and excluding the unanimous baseline trials 1-4, where both theories make identical predictions and which would only dilute the contrast.

Predicted values (using mid-range parameters): OCO-LI gives exactly 0.50 on the eight m=2 split-tie pairs (parameter-free, since the flat tally is 1/1 and the guess mixture preserves 0.5), ~0.41 on the m=3 pairs (tally 2:1 against the late row) and ~0.39 on the m=4 pairs (tally 3:1 against the late row), for an overall value near 0.46-0.47. RDS gives ~0.70-0.86 on the m=2 pairs, ~0.78 on m=3 and ~0.72 on m=4, overall near 0.79. That is a ~0.32 gap.

Precision is high because the metric pools 72 trials per subject (12 unique pairs x 6 reps), so per-subject binomial noise is ~0.06 SD, and OCO-LI's dominant component (the m=2 ties at exactly 0.5) is completely parameter-independent, keeping between-subject variance tiny. Direction of the metric is not trivially tied to either model's mechanism label: it is a purely descriptive 'last-differing-row' choice rate that any theory can be scored on.

The two theories share everything except OCO-LI's label-individuation gate, which in this near-duplicate-validity design forces phi ~ 0.16, i.e. ~85% probability matching to the raw proportion of discriminating rows. So the decisive question is: on trials where the row-count tally and the single most salient (late, low-validity) discriminating row point in different directions (or the tally is exactly tied and thus uninformative), do choices follow the salient row or hug the tally?

The metric selects exactly those conflict trials (tally tied, or tally majority opposite to the highest-salience discriminating row, using the design's known validities with lam=1.6, delta=0.9) and reports the proportion of choices that follow the salient-row owner. This selection automatically drops the two unanimous baseline bases (where both models agree) and keeps bases 3-9, ~70 of 90 trials per subject, so the metric is tight per subject (binomial with ~70 observations).

Quantitative predictions from the two generative models with central parameters: RDS ~ 0.73-0.76 (salience essentially owns the decision; only the conflict-interference lapse pulls it down), OCO-LI ~ 0.50 (its 84% ungated component is pinned to the tally, which by construction opposes or is neutral w.r.t. the salient row). A ~0.24 gap with per-subject SD around 0.05-0.07 gives a very large Welch t at N=25. The metric is also mirror-symmetric (each base appears with its A/B mirror), so side bias cannot inflate or deflate it.

Both theories agree on the *form* of row salience (late position x low validity), so the only thing that separates them is whether that salience DECIDES the trial (SSI-DS+ sums the rescaled weights and passes them through a steep sigmoid, so the single dominant late/low-validity row saturates the choice) or merely wins a rarely-run anchoring competition (OCO-LI: the label-individuation gate is pinned near phi ~= 0.13 by the 0.004 label spacing, so ~87% of the time the choice is a probability-matched tally of discriminating rows, which sits near chance on these conflict displays and can even oppose the salient row when it is outvoted).

The metric restricts to CONFLICT displays (bases 3-8; unanimous dominance trials are excluded because both models predict ~0.86 there and would only dilute the contrast) and scores the proportion of choices agreeing with the single most salient discriminating row under the shared salience form. Hand-computed predictions at the designs' nominal parameters: OCO-LI gives 0.51, 0.55, 0.45, 0.43, 0.43, 0.53 across the six conflict bases -> pooled ~0.48 (i.e. essentially chance, since the tally usually rules); SSI-DS+ gives 0.73, 0.86, 0.78, 0.72, 0.67, 0.72 -> pooled ~0.75 (saturated on the dominant row). A ~0.27 gap over 72 trials per subject means per-subject binomial SD ~0.06, so the contrast is both large in mean and tight within subject.

Crucially this is not trivially true of my theory: OCO-LI *does* contain the same anti-validity/recency salience, and if the gate were all-or-none (or absent) OCO-LI would also score high here. Near-chance salience-consistency on conflict displays is the specific fingerprint of a graded label-individuation gate plus one-reason (non-summing) anchoring.

Both theories agree on the DIRECTION of preference on every conflict display in this design (the side carrying the larger salience mass), so a direction-agnostic accuracy score is not trivially true for either model; what differs is the DECISIVENESS with which that side is chosen. SSI-DS+ maps evidence through sigmoid(beta * (S_A - S_B)/max_row), which saturates and is strongly boosted whenever the winning side is a coalition of sub-maximal rows; OCO-LI maps it to the raw salience SHARE S_A/(S_A+S_B), which is bounded and near-linear, hence much closer to chance on exactly these displays. Restricting to conflict displays (min(n_A,n_B) >= 1) excludes the unanimous trials where the two accounts nearly coincide (they differ only via eta), so the metric concentrates all trials where the gap is largest. Trial-by-trial hand computation with central parameter values gives an expected pooled score of ~0.75 under SSI-DS+ versus ~0.63 under OCO-LI (largest per-pair gaps at the coalition trials 11/12: .74 vs .56, and 15/16: .71 vs .55). Because the score aggregates ~72 trials per subject and only mildly depends on the free parameters (eps0/rho/beta shift it by ~0.02-0.03), per-subject variance should be ~0.003-0.004, giving a Welch t of roughly 6-7 at N=25.

The metric is a pure choice-key agreement score restricted to the trial types on which the two theories make OPPOSITE binary predictions. For each trial I recompute (a) MDSC-NV's near-argmax maximum-doubt winner (the verdict of the single most doubtful discriminating expert, log u = 15*log(1-v) + 1.725*j) and (b) SSI-DS+'s compensatory summation winner (sign of sum of sign*(1-v)^0.9*exp(1.5*j)). On this design the two orderings cross at the extremes (col0, v=.55, is MDSC's #2 but SSI's last; col5, v=.85, is SSI's #1 but MDSC's #4), so 8 of the 16 pairs (trials 4,5,6,8 and their exact mirrors 12,13,14,16 => 48 of 96 trials per subject) are diagnostic and key-balanced (4 favour A, 4 favour B), so response bias cannot inflate the score. Hand-computing the generative probabilities: MDSC-NV gives p(its own key) ~ .75 (t4/t12), ~.72 (t5/t13), ~.62 (t6/t14, the lone doubtful row beating a 5-row coalition), ~.75 (t8/t16), i.e. an expected metric value ~.71; SSI-DS+ gives ~.14, ~.15, ~.39, ~.32, i.e. ~.25. Gap ~.46. Because the score averages 48 trials per subject and the free parameters (q, eps0, rho, beta, gamma) only shift these probabilities by a few points, per-subject SD should be ~.07-.08 (var ~.006), giving a Welch t of roughly 15-20 at N=25. The metric also mirrors the two key qualitative claims: doubt beats recency (early .55 / mid .90 rows outvoting late .85/.95 rows) and coalitions buy nothing (1 row beating 5).

The design contains six base structures (D, E, F, G, H, K) on which SSI-DS+ and MDSC-NV point to OPPOSITE options: SSI-DS+ sums max-normalised weights that are dominated by the late, high-validity rows, while MDSC-NV lets the single most doubtful (lowest-validity) discriminating row decide, with coalitions buying nothing. The metric selects exactly those conflict trials online (by recomputing the two decision rules per trial from the stimulus, using each theory's central parameter values) and reports the proportion of choices that went to the SSI-DS+ favoured option. Unanimous displays, base J (where both rules agree), and any trial where the rules coincide are excluded automatically, so the metric is not trivially true for either account: it is a pure directional read-out of 'weighted late-row summation' vs 'anti-validity single cue'. Expected value under SSI-DS+ is roughly 0.75-0.78 (average of .86, .86, .64, .80, .73, .68 across bases D, E, F, G, H, K) and under MDSC-NV roughly 0.25 (average of .12, .28, .34, .19, .25, .35) \u2014 a ~0.5 gap. Because ~48 trials per subject enter the average, binomial noise is only ~0.06 SD and parameter heterogeneity is modest (both models' lapse terms are bounded), so the per-subject spread should be far below the between-theory gap.

This isolates the design's Block-2/Block-3 coalition displays in which the single .68 expert (feature 0) dissents against a coalition of two or three MORE valid experts (features 1, 2, 4) while the .52 anchor (feature 3) is silent \u2014 i.e. base structures 6 and 7 (trial pairs 11-14), 20 trials per subject.

MDSC-NV is a near-argmax maximum-doubt one-reason rule: the least valid DISCRIMINATING expert (.68) decides regardless of how many more valid experts oppose it, and capture by the silent .52 anchor only pulls part of the way toward chance. It therefore predicts the lone .68 dissenter's option is still chosen well ABOVE chance (~.64-.67).

DTV-RG/CL, because the least valid dissenter (.68) is ABOVE its absolute-doubt trigger (v_c \u2248 .575), flips into near-tally mode (\u03c6 \u2248 .88), so a 2- or 3-member coalition of more valid experts overturns the lone dissenter: it predicts this same quantity CRASHES BELOW chance (~.23-.27).

So the predicted values are ~.65 vs ~.25 \u2014 a ~40-point gap that straddles chance, with each subject contributing 20 trials, giving tight per-subject estimates (binomial SD \u2248 .10) and a clean Welch separation at N=25. It is not trivially true of MDSC: a compensatory model, a pure tally, a recency rule, or any ordinary take-the-best (which would favour the most valid expert's side) all give distinct values, and the contrast is purely about whether coalitions of more valid experts can overturn one doubtful dissenter.

This isolates Block 2's 'coalition crash' cells (trial pairs 11-14: 1-vs-2 and 1-vs-3 displays in which the lone dissenter is c0 = .62, the least valid DISCRIMINATING expert, while the globally most doubtful expert c4 = .53 stays SILENT). The metric is the proportion of those trials on which the subject sides with the lone least-valid dissenter.

DTV-RG/CL: with the sub-trigger .53 expert silent, v0 = .62 > v_c, so phi jumps to ~.85 and evidence becomes a near-tally rank-geometric sum: E = 1 - phi - phi^2 (1-vs-2) and 1 - phi - phi^2 - phi^3 (1-vs-3), both clearly NEGATIVE at every corner of the parameter box. The coalition of more valid experts overturns the lone dissenter, so choice falls BELOW chance: predicted ~.24-.27.

MDSC-NV: the doubt rule is near-argmax over discriminating rows, and c0 (.62) is by far the most doubtful discriminating row, so the deliberate route almost always sides with the lone dissenter; only the capture-to-silent-row component (q ~ .41 x 0.5) and the load lapse pull it toward chance, leaving it clearly ABOVE chance: predicted ~.65-.68.

Hence a ~0.41 directional gap that straddles chance, with 16 trials per subject and parameter ranges that barely move either prediction, so between-subject variance is dominated by (small) binomial noise. The metric uses no theory-specific machinery: it is just 'do people follow the lone least-valid dissenter against a coalition?'

The design's decisive contrast is whether the option backed by the single most doubtful expert (column 3, validity .55) survives when an opposing coalition of slightly-less-doubtful experts (c2 .62, c4 .70, c5 .74) speaks against it. I select exactly those trials in which the .55 expert discriminates AND at least one row favours the other option (base structures 2, 3, 4, 5 and 8: 1-vs-1, 1-vs-2, 1-vs-3, 2-vs-2, 1-vs-5), and score the proportion of choices that follow the .55 anchor. MDSC-NV (near-argmax single-cue on doubt, delta 13-17) says coalitions buy essentially nothing: the anchor's core probability stays .96-.99 in every one of these cells and only the load lapse pulls the observed rate down, giving an expected anchor-follow rate around .72-.80. NAVA-HLp's divisive compensatory summation gives the coalition rows normalized weights of ~.49-.60 each, so two or three of them sum past 1 and flip the sign of E, predicting anchor-follow rates around .41-.50 (i.e. below chance) on most of these cells and ~.48 pooled. The predicted gap is therefore roughly .27-.30 with the two theories straddling chance in opposite directions. Because the metric aggregates ~30 unique-trial repetitions per subject (5 base structures x 2 mirrors x 6 reps = 60 trials) the binomial noise per subject is ~.06 SD and the only additional between-subject spread comes from lapse parameters (a few points), so the contrast should be both large and tight. The metric is well-defined on a single subject's slice and on the pooled frame alike, and it is not trivially true of MDSC-NV: any compensatory or tally-like process (including the competitor) would put it at or below .5.

The decisive axis between NAVA-HLp (compensatory divisive summation) and MDSC-NV (near-argmax single-cue doubt selection) is whether the WEIGHT of the opposing rows enters the decision at all. I isolate exactly the coalition displays in which the most-doubtful expert (column 0, v=.52 \u2014 MDSC's doubt argmax at every corner of its parameter box) discriminates and is opposed by at least two of the slightly-less-doubtful late rows (c3=.78, c4=.80, c5=.83). This selection picks out bases 6, 7, 8, 9 and 12 of the design (trials 11/12, 13/14, 15/16, 17/18, 23/24), i.e. 10 unique pairs \u00d7 4 reps = 40 trials per subject \u2014 enough to keep binomial noise per subject small (~.006 variance).

The metric is the proportion of those trials on which the subject picks the option endorsed by the .52 anchor. Hand-computing both generative models at mid-box parameters: NAVA gives .452, .404, .427, .472, .439 across the five bases (mean \u2248 .44 \u2014 BELOW chance, because \u03a3\u0175 of the opposing coalition exceeds 1 and normalization lets it overturn the anchor), whereas MDSC gives .806, .747, .662, .747, .662 (mean \u2248 .73 \u2014 always ABOVE chance, because only the identity of the doubt argmax matters and coalitions buy nothing; only the load lapse pulls it toward .5). The gap is ~.29 with a directional split across chance, so it cannot be mimicked by differences in lapse rate, side bias, or general anti-validity tendency: both theories are anti-validity, both charge load, and mirrored A/B versions of every base are included so side bias cancels exactly. Per-subject parameter heterogeneity moves each theory only within its own corner range (NAVA .33\u2013.61, MDSC .66\u2013.84), leaving the two distributions essentially non-overlapping at N=25.

This isolates the 'coalitions buy nothing vs. compensatory summation' cell (design bases 9-12, pairs 17-24; 32 trials/subject). Selection rule: the .52 anchor expert (index 4) is silent, the mid-doubt .66 expert (index 5) discriminates, and at least one MORE valid expert (indices 0-3, validities .70/.96/.64/.88) opposes it. The metric is the rate of choosing the option backed by the single .66 expert against that opposing coalition.

MDSC-NV: with the anchor silent, the doubt argmax among discriminating rows is c5 (.66), leading by 0.21-0.36 log-units, so with a near-argmax doubt gain the verdict of c5 decides the trial; extra opposing rows only add a load leak and null-verdict capture drags things partway toward chance. Predicted ~.64-.72 pooled (~.67), reliably ABOVE chance in every included cell.

DTG-2R/OC: .66 is above the absolute sharp trigger (g<=.004), so all these displays fall into the compensatory limb, where the normalised anti-validity weights of c2 (.80), c0 (.46), c3 (.08) sum against c5 (1.0) and the k_conf/load leaks flatten the result. Predicted ~.47-.53 pooled (~.49), i.e. essentially AT or BELOW chance.

So the two theories straddle chance with a ~.18-.19 gap, while each subject contributes 32 trials (binomial SD ~.09) and the parameter boxes produce only ~.03 of extra between-subject spread, giving a tight, large-N-robust contrast. Neither value is trivially fixed by my model's machinery: it is an empirical question whether a lone mediocre dissenter beats a coalition of more valid experts.

The two theories agree on WHICH row carries the verdict in every display of this design; they disagree about (i) whether long displays are cheap when the .52 anchor speaks, and (ii) whether a merely mid-doubt lone dissenter (.68) still dictates the choice when the anchor is silent.

The metric is a within-subject difference of two rates computed from the stimulus structure alone (no theory-specific fitting):

T = P(choose the option favoured by the .52 anchor) on LONG, low-opposition displays (anchor discriminates, m>=4 discriminating rows, at most one row in the minority) -> trials 3, 6, 11, 15, 18, 23 (24 trials/subject).
C = P(choose the option favoured by the .68 last-column row) when the .52 anchor is SILENT and the .68 row stands ALONE against a coalition of 1-3 more valid rows -> trials 7, 8, 9, 19, 20, 21 (24 trials/subject).

DTG-2R/OC-sharp: the one-reason limb is charged for opposition, not for list length, so T stays high (~.85) even at m=6; and with no sub-threshold expert discriminating, the compensatory limb (anti-validity weights normalised to the loudest dissent, load-degraded) pulls C to or below chance (~.47-.52). Predicted T - C ~ +0.35.

MDSC-NV: the load leak rho^(m-2) drags long displays down (T ~ .66-.74) while near-argmax doubt keeps the .68-holder chosen well above chance (C ~ .65-.72). Predicted T - C ~ 0.00.

Both components use 24 trials per subject, so binomial noise is modest, and both theories' predicted rates are driven by parameters with narrow ranges, keeping between-subject variance small relative to the ~0.35 mean gap. A near-zero value falsifies the absolute sharp doubt gate + opposition-costed one-reason limb; a large positive value falsifies MDSC-NV.
